```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 100)
library(peopleparser)
```

The same person often appears under different forms of their first name:
ROBERT one year, BOB the next, then ROBERT again. peopleparser can attach to
each parsed name its formal names, its nicknames, and one **canonical first
name**, a single form shared by the variants of a name. This article explains
where the variants come from, how the canonical name is chosen when a name has
several possible formal names, and how gender is used to decide between them.

## The variant table

`first_name_pairs` holds pairs of first names that are two forms of one
given name. The pairs come from the **synthid** package. synthid follows each
person on a Form 990 Part VII list across their own organization's filings,
2010-2024 (15.0 million people), and records the first-name forms each person
used. A person listed as ROBERT, BOB and ROB gives three pairs. The synthid
vignette *First-name variants - how the table was built* describes the build
and the hand review.

```{r}
table(first_name_pairs$type, first_name_pairs$lexicon)
```

* The **lexicon** (`lexicon = TRUE`) is 1,002 pairs seen in 25 or more
  people, reviewed by hand: nicknames (BOB/ROBERT), spellings
  (STEVEN/STEPHEN), cognates (JOSE/JOSEPH) and compound names (MARY/MARYANN).
* The other rows were not reviewed. **Misspellings** pair a rare form with a
  common one (KATHRINE/CATHERINE). **Sound-alikes** pair two established names
  that sound the same (KRISTY/KRISTIE).

Each row records how many people carry the pair (`n_emp_ids`), how common each
form is nationally (`freq_short`, `freq_long`) and the share of each form's
records that are female (`f_short`, `f_long`).

```{r}
subset(first_name_pairs, name_short %in% c("PAT", "KATE") & lexicon,
       c(name_short, name_long, type, n_emp_ids, f_short, f_long, formal)) |> knitr::kable()
```

Pairs are stored with the shorter form first. That is not always the formal
name (JOHN/JOHNNY, DEBRA/DEBBIE), so the `formal` column says which side of a
nickname pair is the formal name. It comes from three rules, in order:

1. a pet ending added to the other form (JOHNNY, BILLY, KATIE from KATE);
2. a pet ending (-Y, -IE, -EY, -I) on a form no longer than the other
   (KATHY/KATHLEEN, CHARLIE/CHARLES);
3. otherwise, the longer form.

Three pairs were corrected by hand after review.

## Chains: why a name cannot simply follow its links

Each pair links two names, so the pairs form chains. In the KATHERINE chain,
24 names are joined by 40 pairs:

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/chain-katherine-pairs.png")
```

Following the links would make every name in the chain one name. KATE is a
nickname of both KATHLEEN and CATHERINE, so KATHLEEN and CATHERINE would be
merged, although they are different names. The canonical rule therefore uses
only **direct** links: a spelling step, then at most one nickname step.

## The canonical rule

### Step 1: spelling root

Spelling pairs (reviewed spellings, plus misspellings whose rare form has fewer
than 1,000 national records) form a graph. Each name moves to its most common
spelling partner, repeatedly, as long as that partner is more common. Each step
goes to a more common name, so the path always ends. Its end is the
**spelling root**:

```{r}
nickname_lookup(c("KATHRYN", "KATHERINE", "STEVEN", "JEFFERY", "KATHRINE"))[
  , c("first_name_canonical", "canonical_rule")] |> knitr::kable()
```

KATHRYN moves to KATHERINE (more common), and KATHERINE to CATHERINE (more
common still). The 1,000-record cap keeps distinct names out: MARCO is listed
as a misspelling of MARK (8,069 records against 591,323), but it is a name in
its own right, so it is not merged.

### Step 2: the nickname step

A name is resolved to a formal name when its spelling family is mainly used as
a nickname. Two tests decide this:

* more people carry the family as the nickname side of a pair than as the
  formal side; and
* the number of people carrying it as a nickname is at least `min_nick_rate`
  (0.2%) of the name's national records.

The second test keeps standalone names standalone. Fifty people carry
MARK/MARCUS, out of 591,323 MARK records (0.008%), so MARK stays MARK. JIM
passes easily: 13,435 people carry JIM/JAMES, 3.7% of the JIM records.

```{r}
canonical_first_name(c("JIM", "MARK", "CHAD", "LISA"))
```

The formal candidates are the name's **direct** formal partners. Partners that
are themselves mostly nicknames are dropped when any other partner exists (KATIE
is not resolved to KATE). The candidates are grouped by spelling root, and each
group is weighted by the people carrying its pairs. The top group wins if it
holds at least `min_share` (60%) of the weight:

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/shares-al.png")
```

ALAN, ALLEN and ALLAN are one name, so they pool their evidence. Even so, 45%
is not enough, so AL is **ambiguous** and keeps its own spelling root. KATHY is
ambiguous for the same reason, split between KATHLEEN and the KATHERINE
spellings. Applied to the KATHERINE chain:

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/chain-katherine-canonical.png")
```

```{r}
x <- c("KATE", "KATIE", "KITTY", "KATHY", "CATHY", "KATHLEEN", "CATHLEEN")
cbind(name = x, nickname_lookup(x, gender = "F", gender_confidence = 99)[
  , c("first_name_type", "first_name_canonical", "canonical_rule")]) |> knitr::kable()
```

`canonical_rule` records how each canonical name was reached:

| rule | meaning |
|---|---|
| `self` | the name is its own canonical form |
| `spelling` | moved to its spelling root |
| `nickname` | resolved through the nickname step |
| `ambiguous` | a nickname whose formal name could not be chosen; kept as its spelling root |

## Gender

Gender is used only to choose among formal names. It does not change spellings
or the names in a family. The gender evidence for a record is:

1. a gendered salutation: `MR` is male; `MRS`, `MS` and `MISS` are female;
2. otherwise, the parsed `gender`, if `gender_confidence` is at least
   `min_confidence` (80);
3. otherwise, unknown.

With known gender, formal candidates of the other gender are dropped. A
candidate's gender is the majority of its national records (`f_long` or
`f_short`). Then the share test is applied to the candidates that remain:

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/gender-pat.png")
```

```{r}
nickname_lookup(c("PAT", "PAT", "PAT"), gender = c("F", "M", "U"),
                gender_confidence = c(95, 95, 50))[
  , c("first_name_formal", "first_name_canonical", "canonical_rule")] |> knitr::kable()
```

If gender rules out **every** candidate, the name keeps its own form (`self`).
The table has no female formal name for CHRIS, so a female CHRIS stays CHRIS
and is not sent to CHRISTOPHER:

```{r}
nickname_lookup("CHRIS", gender = "F", gender_confidence = 95)[
  , c("first_name_formal", "first_name_canonical", "canonical_rule")] |> knitr::kable()
```

**A caution about gender.** The `gender` field in a parse is itself inferred
from the first name (census name frequencies), and so is the female share
recorded in the variant table. 99.8% of PAT records in the table are female.
A parse of PAT says female with only 60% confidence. That is below the
threshold of 80, so PAT alone stays ambiguous. PAT resolves to a formal name
only when a salutation gives the gender. The `gender` column of the parse
does not use the salutation (MR PAT still reads F there); the nickname step
does:

```{r}
parse_names(c("PAT SMITH", "MR PAT SMITH", "MRS PAT SMITH"), add_nicknames = TRUE)[
  , c("name", "gender", "gender_confidence", "first_name_canonical", "canonical_rule")] |> knitr::kable()
```

## A name's whole family: `first_name_variants()`

`first_name_variants()` lists everything that shares a name's canonical form,
and how each name gets there. `via` is the name it connects through. Rows with
`in_canonical = FALSE` are related but **not** merged:

* unreviewed sound-alikes;
* cognates (JOSE for JOSEPH) and compounds (MARYANN);
* nicknames that are ambiguous between this name and another.

```{r}
first_name_variants("kate", min_freq = 1000) |> knitr::kable()
```

KATE resolves to CATHERINE. The family holds CATHERINE's spellings, the
misspellings that lead to them, and its nicknames. KATHY and CATHY appear as
ambiguous nicknames: they could belong to this family, but they are not merged
into it.

Without the related rows and the rare forms:

```{r}
first_name_variants("steve", related = FALSE, min_freq = 100) |> knitr::kable()
```

Gender can change the family. For a female PAT the family is PATRICIA. With
no gender PAT is ambiguous, so its family is just PAT:

```{r}
first_name_variants("pat", gender = "F", min_freq = 1000) |> knitr::kable()
first_name_variants("pat", min_freq = 1000) |> knitr::kable()
```

## Using it when parsing

`parse_name()` and `parse_names()` take `add_nicknames = TRUE`, which adds the
columns `first_name_type`, `first_name_formal`, `first_name_nicknames`,
`first_name_canonical` and `canonical_rule`:

```{r}
x <- c("Bob Jones", "MRS PAT LEE", "Kathy Ruiz", "STEVEN H PARK", "Mark Webb")
parse_names(x, add_nicknames = TRUE)[
  , c("name", "first_name", "gender", "first_name_formal", "first_name_canonical",
      "canonical_rule")] |> knitr::kable()
```

The helpers `canonical_first_name()`, `get_formal_names()` and
`get_nicknames()` return single columns of the same lookup.

## How well it works

A pilot on 33,535 Part VII records (1,000 organizations, 2010-2012) that
synthid had linked into persons compared the canonical name with synthid's
earlier 70-name nickname table (`data-raw/pilot-nicknames/`):

| | Same person, first names differ (204 pairs) | Different people, same return and year (per 1,000 pairs) |
|---|---:|---:|
| 70-name table, direct pairs | 56% matched | 2.2 |
| same canonical name | 83% matched | 2.9 |
| same canonical name, or a lexicon pair | 89% matched | 3.4 |

* For 93% of the people seen under both a nickname and its formal name, the
  two names get the same canonical name.
* About a quarter of records change name. 1.2% are ambiguous.
* Most same-person pairs still missed are typos (MARAGARET, STEPHEM), which a
  string-distance comparison handles.
* Most different-person "matches" are two people with one name on the same
  board (JIM and JAMES), which only the surname and other fields can separate.

The same-person figures are optimistic. The variant table was built from the
same kind of person links, so this test is partly circular. The
different-person test does not have that problem.

## Settings

| argument | default | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `min_share` | 0.6 | share of the evidence the top formal name needs; lower resolves more ambiguous nicknames |
| `min_nick_rate` | 0.002 | how much nickname use a name needs before it is resolved; 0 lets MARK resolve to MARCUS |
| `spelling` | `c("lexicon", "misspelling")` | add `"sound_alike"` to merge unreviewed sound-alikes too |
| `min_confidence` | 80 | census gender confidence needed to use `gender` |
